rv.q: Its last few minutes feel like staring overwhelmed at the secrets of creation.
...utterly absorbing piece from avant-garde performance makers Complicité
Mnemonic is still a teeming, fecund representation of McBurney’s ability to make giant associative leaps while drilling down into what makes us human.
This remains unique experimental theatre, which will linger in the mind long after its conclusion.

The applause that greeted the end of Mnemonic on opening night was reverential rather than ecstatic, a fitting response to a piece of theatre whose legendary status outshines the actual experience of watching it.
It is as if, with all these exquisite parts, the production does not quite deliver on a promise of profundity in tying them together.
In a repertoire of so many inspired pieces, few shine as memorably as Mnemonic.
As well as being enormously thoughtful, it’s at times very funny.

Complicité’s MNEMONIC staged at the National in 2001, underwent a reimagining and dusting-off in readiness for this summer’s repeat run at the Olivier, retaining Simon McBurney’s all-important creative micro-vision as he serves once more as Director on the production.
Mnemonic made a lasting impression on me at the start of this century, and it has again as we hurtle hesitantly but also, on this evidence, beautifully through it.
And it is clear that a quarter of a century on, no one builds a technical and cinematic story quite like Complicité.
The problem with the show proper is that while it is ambitious, it is also fragmented.
Without the vital humanity beating at its core, the production doesn't connect all the dots.

cn.t: Complicité's cerebral revival earns respect for its ambitious exploration of memory and migration, though critics split on whether this 25-year-old experimental piece still resonates or feels dated for contemporary audiences.
